blocks.text: Cf. STORR, Observatt. ad Analog. et Syntax. Hebr. p. 383 ff.

Parallel passages (παράλληλα [parallēla]) from the Arab poets and their commentators will be supplied by SCHULTENS in his Commentar. on the passage, p. 1120, 1121, 1122, who should by all means be read, since you will also find there the opinions of others weighed. Nor will you regret comparing SHAW, Itinerar. p. 388 ff., German trans., Leipzig 1765. He illustrates the whole passage of Job with what he himself observed, and confirms by his own testimony what Bochart brought forward from the books of the Arabs. The fable of the ostrich hatching its eggs by the mere gaze of its eyes is reported from Giauhari by WANSLEBEN in his Itinerarium, edited by Paulus in the Sylloge of Itineraries, vol. 3, p. 186. Nor should what Paulus remarked on it in the Notes at the end of the book, p. 395, be passed over.
Schultens excerpted the passage from Firuzabadi, p. 1124.

But ALB. SCHULTENS, p. 1126, renders it more correctly: it urges itself on to running. For the verb مري [marā] means he drove a horse to a faster run by striking it with the whip. Giauhari: مريت الفرس اذا استخرجت ما عنده من الجري بسوط او غيره [maraytu al-faras idhā istakhrajtu mā ʿindahu min al-jary bi-sawṭ aw ghayrihi] One says מריח אלפרש I urged the horse, when I draw out, by applying the whip, or something else (spurs), whatever it has in running. This verb is indeed most aptly used by the Hebrew poet. For the ostrich, as Shaw testifies (p. 387, German trans.), has under its wings a small claw with which it wounds itself as it runs harder, and so draws blood. Bochart too notes this very thing below, at the end of our chapter.
Schultens presents similar passages from the Arab poets, p. 1227.
